questions.q: Why does this lesson describe Performance Troubleshooting's Slow Request Log and Script Performance Profiler as "reactive" tools?
options: They diagnose and fix a performance problem only after it has already degraded the instance
They only work on tables that have never been indexed
They cannot be used by anyone outside the architecture review board
They were deprecated in favor of proactive architecture reviews
questions.explain: Reactive tools find a problem that already exists; the architect's job is to make design-time decisions that prevent that problem from happening in the first place.

questions.q: Why is retrofitting an index onto a live, already-slow table more expensive than deciding the indexing strategy upfront?
options: It requires a schema change against live production data, consumes resources to re-index, and means users already experienced the slow symptoms for months
ServiceNow does not allow indexes to be added after a table is created
Retrofitted indexes are always functionally incorrect
It has no real cost difference compared to designing the index upfront
questions.explain: Chapter 3's upfront table-and-indexing design avoids exactly this cost: a live schema change plus months of users already feeling the slowdown.

questions.q: Why can choosing a synchronous request-response integration pattern without modeling anticipated volume become a performance problem?
options: Each request holds a semaphore for the duration of the call, and a pattern that works fine at low volume can become the platform's primary bottleneck at high volume
Request-response integrations never hold a semaphore at all
Event-driven integrations are always slower than request-response at any volume
Anticipated volume has no effect on which integration pattern is appropriate
questions.explain: This is the same semaphore-contention mechanism Performance Troubleshooting's "Semaphore & Node Usage" lesson diagnoses after the fact — here it's prevented by choosing the pattern with real volume projections at design time.

questions.q: What specific anti-patterns does a performance-focused code review standard check for, per this lesson?
options: Unbounded GlideRecord queries inside a loop, recursive Business Rule triggers, and queries with no encoded filter driving a full table scan
Only whether a script include uses correct JavaScript syntax
Whether a Business Rule's name follows a naming convention
Whether a table has a description field filled in
questions.explain: These are the exact anti-patterns taught in "GlideRecord Performance Pitfalls" and "Common Business Rule Mistakes" — a review standard catches them before they reach production.

questions.q: What is the architect's real leverage in a code review standard that catches performance anti-patterns before merge, per this lesson?
options: Mandating that the checklist exists and is actually enforced, not personally writing every line of review feedback
Personally reviewing every single pull request on the platform
Replacing the Script Performance Profiler entirely so it's never needed again
Removing GlideRecord from the list of approved server-side APIs
questions.explain: The architect's leverage is organizational: requiring that a real, enforced review standard exists, not personally catching every anti-pattern by hand.
